frontmatter.name: safe-updates
frontmatter.description: Update WordPress plugins, themes and core without breaking the site, and repair a site that broke after an update. Use when asked to update or upgrade anything, to say whether an update is safe, or when the site shows an error, a blank page or missing content after an update.

name: safe-updates
description: Update WordPress plugins, themes and core without breaking the site, and repair a site that broke after an update. Use when asked to update or upgrade anything, to say whether an update is safe, or when the site shows an error, a blank page or missing content after an update.
metadata:
  version: "1"
---

# Safe updates

An update replaces code that runs on every page. Most go in cleanly. Some break the
site, and one that breaks every request also cuts this connection, so it cannot be
fixed from here afterwards. Work in the order below.

## Rules

- One update at a time. Run the two-call check of step 5 after each one, before the next.
- Never send the same update call twice. When a call fails, times out or answers with
  a maintenance message, read the installed version first (`wp_list_plugins`,
  `wp_list_themes`) and decide from that.
- Never delete or uninstall anything. Do not switch the active theme to fix an update.
- Do only what was asked. A question ("is it safe?") is answered without changing
  anything. A repair request ("it broke") is not a request to install other updates.
- When the server says a tool is not available to this connection, do not work
  around it. Say which tool is switched off and how the user does that step in
  wp-admin.
- Never report a step as done unless the tool's reply shows it.

## Steps

1. **Inventory.** Call `wp_list_plugin_updates`, and `wp_list_themes` when themes are in
   scope. For WordPress itself, `wp_get_site_health` names a pending core release.
   Note for each update: installed and new version, `requires_php`, `requires`, and
   `package_available`.
2. **Baseline.** Before the first update, run the check of step 5 once: Site Health,
   then the log. Keep the log's last line, and note whether the home page answered
   normally. Anything wrong at this point is not caused by your updates; tell the user
   about it before you start.
3. **Rate each update** with `references/risk.md` (call `wp_get_skill` with this skill's
   name and that file). In short: an update that cannot be installed from here is
   reported, not attempted; a patch release is low risk; a major version, WordPress
   core, and any plugin the site's sales or logins depend on are high risk.
4. **Backup.** If the user has not said they have a recent backup, install only the
   low-risk updates and hold the high-risk ones: list them under "Needs you" and say a
   backup is the reason. If the user confirmed a backup, install everything, low risk
   first, WordPress core last. Before the first update, tell the user in one sentence
   what to do if the site stops answering (see `references/recovery.md`).
5. **Update and check, one at a time.** Call `wp_update_plugin` (or `wp_update_theme`,
   `wp_update_core`). Then run this check: both calls, after every single update, the
   last one included. Send them one after the other, never together: wait for the
   Site Health reply before reading the log. Reading the log alone, or at the same
   moment, proves nothing, because an error on a page is only written when something
   loads that page.
   1. `wp_get_site_health` with `include_async: true`. The server loads the home page
      while it runs. A test in the reply that says the home page answered with an
      error status (HTTP 500 or similar) means this update broke the site.
   2. `wp_get_error_log`, compared with the baseline. A new line that says "Fatal
      error", "Uncaught" or "Parse error" and names the plugin's or theme's folder
      means this update broke the site. Warnings and deprecation notices do not.
6. **If it broke, undo that one update at once.** A home page that answered normally at
   the baseline and answers with an error status after an update was broken by that
   update, even when the log shows nothing. Do not stop to ask: the site is down until
   you undo it, and both ways of undoing are reversible. Then carry on with the other
   updates.
   - A plugin or theme from wordpress.org: call the update tool again with `version`
     set to the version it had before.
   - Anything else: call `wp_deactivate_plugin`. The plugin's feature is off until the
     user installs a working version.
   - Repeat the check from step 5 until the log is quiet, then continue with the
     remaining updates.
7. **Finish.** Call `wp_clear_cache` with `scope: "site"` if any update was installed.

For a site that is already broken, skip to `references/recovery.md`.

## Report

End with these four headings, in this order, leaving out a heading that is empty:

- **Updated**: name, old version → new version.
- **Rolled back or deactivated**: name, what failed (quote the log line), what state it
  is in now.
- **Skipped**: name and the reason (needs a licence, needs a newer PHP, package
  missing, tool switched off).
- **Needs you**: what the user has to do, in wp-admin terms, and anything held for a
  backup.

# Recovery

## The site is already broken and this connection still works

1. Call `wp_get_error_log`. Look for the newest "Fatal error", "Uncaught" or "Parse
   error" line. Its file path names the plugin or theme folder that fails.
2. If the log has nothing recent, call `wp_get_site_health` with `include_async: true`
   (the server loads the home page), then read the log again.
3. Call `wp_list_plugins` to confirm the version of the plugin the path names.
4. Undo it: for a wordpress.org plugin or theme, the update tool with `version` set to
   the previous version; otherwise `wp_deactivate_plugin`.
5. Check again as in step 2. Only say the site works when the log stays quiet.
6. Do not install other pending updates. The user asked for a repair.

## What to tell the user before the first risky update

One sentence is enough: "If the site stops loading during this, open wp-admin; if that
fails too, use the recovery link WordPress emails to the site administrator, or rename
the plugin's folder over SFTP or the host's file manager, which switches it off."

## The connection stops answering after an update

You cannot reach the site any more. Do not keep retrying the update. Tell the user:

1. Which plugin or theme was being updated, from which version to which.
2. WordPress emails the administrator a recovery-mode link when a plugin fails; that
   link opens wp-admin with the failing plugin paused.
3. Without the email: rename `wp-content/plugins/<folder>` over SFTP or the host's
   file manager. WordPress then deactivates it and the site loads.
4. A page that says "Briefly unavailable for scheduled maintenance" for more than ten
   minutes means an update was interrupted: delete the `.maintenance` file in the
   WordPress folder.
5. The host's backup restore is the last resort.

## After a core update

If wp-admin asks for a database update, the WP-CLI tool `wp_cli_run` with
`core update-db` does it when that tool is available; otherwise the user clicks the
button wp-admin shows.

# Rating one update

Read these from `wp_list_plugin_updates` / `wp_list_themes` and from the Site Health
info (`wp_get_site_health`: the server's PHP and WordPress versions).

## Cannot be installed from here: report, do not attempt

| Sign | Say |
|---|---|
| `package_available` is false | The update needs a licence key or a manual download from the vendor. The user installs it in wp-admin (Plugins, or the vendor's own licence screen). |
| `requires_php` is newer than the server's PHP | WordPress would refuse the update. The hosting account has to move to that PHP version first. |
| `requires` is newer than the installed WordPress | WordPress has to be updated first. |
| The update tool is not available to this connection | Which tool is switched off, and that an administrator can switch it on or update from Dashboard › Updates. |

## Low risk: install

- A patch release: only the third number changes (2.4.1 → 2.4.2).
- A security release of any size. Security fixes go first.

## High risk: hold unless the user confirmed a backup

- A major version: the first number changes (2.9.4 → 3.0.0).
- WordPress core, other than a patch release of the installed branch.
- A minor or major release of a plugin the site's sales, logins or page layout depend
  on: a shop, payments, memberships, a page builder, a cache or security plugin.
- A theme whose files were edited on the site (the update overwrites them).

Everything in between (a minor release of an ordinary plugin) is installed, after the
low-risk ones.

frontmatter.name: site-health-review
frontmatter.description: Review a WordPress site's health and report what needs attention - Site Health results, PHP errors, scheduled tasks, and plugin and theme updates. Use when asked to check, audit or review a site, or to find out why it is slow or broken.

files.text:
---
name: site-health-review
description: Review a WordPress site's health and report what needs attention - Site Health results, PHP errors, scheduled tasks, and plugin and theme updates. Use when asked to check, audit or review a site, or to find out why it is slow or broken.
metadata:
  version: "1"
---

# Site health review

This review is read-only. Do not change anything while doing it. List the fixes
and let the user decide which to apply.

## Steps

1. Call `wp_get_site_health` with `include_async` true. Note every critical
   item, then every recommended item, with the test's own label.
2. Call `wp_get_error_log` for recent PHP errors. Group repeated errors and
   name the plugin or theme each one comes from, judging by the file path. If
   the log is unavailable, say so and move on.
3. Call `wp_list_cron_events`. Flag events whose next run is more than an hour
   in the past, and hooks that are scheduled many times over.
4. Call `wp_list_plugin_updates`, then `wp_list_plugins`. Flag pending updates
   and plugins that are installed but inactive.
5. Call `wp_list_themes`. Flag a pending theme update and themes that are
   installed but unused.

If the server reports that a tool is not available to this connection, skip
that step and say which step you skipped and why.

## Report

Write three sections, in this order:

- **Fix now**: critical Site Health items, fatal or frequent PHP errors,
  security updates.
- **Fix soon**: other updates, overdue scheduled tasks, recommended Site Health
  items.
- **For information**: inactive plugins, unused themes, anything else worth
  knowing.

For each item give what is wrong, the evidence (which step and what it
returned), and the fix you suggest. Do not apply any fix in this review.
